_meta.title: Insomnia clinical guideline excerpts (US/international, EN)
sources: Sateia, M. J., Buysse, D. J., Krystal, A. D., Neubauer, D. N., & Heald, J. L. (2017). Clinical Practice Guideline for the Pharmacologic Treatment of Chronic Insomnia in Adults: An American Academy of Sleep Medicine (AASM) Clinical Practice Guideline. J Clin Sleep Med.
Qaseem, A., et al. (2016). Management of Chronic Insomnia Disorder in Adults: A Clinical Practice Guideline From the American College of Physicians (ACP). Ann Intern Med.
American Academy of Sleep Medicine. (2014/2023). International Classification of Sleep Disorders (ICSD-3, 3rd ed.).
_meta.license: Specialty consensus guidelines are public-domain reference content; excerpts used for psychoeducation and AI grounding. Not medical advice — refer users with serious/chronic insomnia to a clinician.

guidelines.summary: Insomnia is dissatisfaction with sleep quantity or quality, causing daytime impairment; ≥3 nights/week for ≥3 months meets chronic insomnia (ICSD-3).
key_points: Difficulty initiating sleep (sleep-onset latency > 30 min)
Difficulty maintaining sleep (wake after sleep onset > 30 min)
Early-morning awakening (waking > 30 min before desired time)
Despite adequate opportunity, sleep remains unsatisfactory
Daytime impairment (fatigue, attention, mood)
guidelines.ai_hint: When users describe duration/awakenings, you can map to this and gently suggest professional evaluation if it sounds chronic.

guidelines.summary: AASM (2017), ACP (2016), and European insomnia guidelines all recommend CBT-I as the **first-line treatment** for adult chronic insomnia — comparable to medication in effect, more durable, and without dependence risk.
key_points: CBT-I components: sleep hygiene, stimulus control, sleep restriction, cognitive restructuring, relaxation training
Standard course is 4–8 weeks; digital CBT-I (dCBT-I) approaches face-to-face outcomes
Effective across age groups, including older adults and those with comorbid anxiety/depression
Pharmacotherapy recommended for short-term or refractory cases only
guidelines.ai_hint: When users ask 'is there anything besides meds?' / 'do I have to take medication?' — cite this as the non-drug first-line evidence.

guidelines.summary: Sleep hygiene is foundational but insufficient on its own for chronic insomnia — pair with other CBT-I components.
key_points: Fixed wake time, including weekends; bedtime may flex
Regular daytime light (especially morning); reduce bright/blue light at night
Avoid caffeine after 14:00 (~5–6 hour half-life)
Avoid alcohol within 3 hours of bedtime (disrupts deep sleep)
Vigorous exercise: not within ~1 hour of bed; regular daytime exercise helps sleep
Bedroom 65–72°F (18–22°C), dim, quiet
Bed for sleep and sex only — the core of stimulus control

guidelines.summary: Re-establish the bed-as-sleep conditioned response (Bootzin, 1972); one of the most evidence-supported single CBT-I components.
key_points: Only get into bed when sleepy
Use bed only for sleep and sex — no work, phones, or worrying
If awake in bed > 20 min: get up, go to another room, do something quiet, return only when sleepy
Fixed wake time daily, regardless of last night's sleep
No daytime napping (older adults may allow ≤30 min)
guidelines.ai_hint: When a user describes 'lying awake forever but doesn't want to get up' — this is the moment for the 20-minute rule.

guidelines.summary: Restrict time in bed to increase sleep efficiency, used in maintenance-type insomnia (Spielman, 1987).
key_points: Initial TIB = mean TST + 30 min (floor 4–5 hours; avoid extremes)
Fixed wake time; bedtime is derived
Weekly review: SE ≥ 90% → expand TIB +15 min; SE < 85% → hold or shrink; 85–90% → hold
First 1–2 weeks may bring more sleepiness/irritability — the 'cost' before benefit
Caution: bipolar mania, uncontrolled seizures, severe circadian disruption, safety-sensitive work (e.g., driving)

guidelines.topic: Signals the AI should gently suggest professional help
guidelines.summary: If any of the following are present, tell the user clearly: 'this is beyond what I can help with — please see a sleep medicine or mental health clinician.'
key_points: Persistent suicidal ideation or self-harm (enter safety protocol immediately)
Persistent severe low mood > 2 weeks + loss of interest (possible depression)
Extreme daytime sleepiness, uncontrollable sleep attacks (possible narcolepsy)
Loud snoring + breathing pauses (possible OSA)
Self-medication with sleeping pills > 1 month or escalating dose
Severe adverse reactions to sleep medication
Severe insomnia during pregnancy or perimenopause
Insomnia > 3 months and self-help CBT-I has not worked
guidelines.ai_hint: This is a non-crisis referral path — distinct from safe_scripts (acute crisis).

guidelines.summary: Short-term/acute insomnia may use BzRA or newer hypnotics briefly; long-term, CBT-I is preferred.
key_points: Medication decisions belong to clinicians — the AI does not recommend specific drugs or doses
Benzodiazepines have dependence and tolerance risk — not recommended chronically
Non-benzodiazepine 'Z-drugs' (zolpidem, eszopiclone, etc.) carry less dependence risk but still short-term-preferred
Melatonin receptor agonists and dual orexin receptor antagonists are options under clinician guidance
If already on medication, never advise stopping abruptly (rebound risk) — clinician-guided taper
guidelines.ai_hint: When users ask 'what should I take?' / 'what dose?' / 'can I stop?' — always defer to a clinician, never name a drug/dose.

guidelines.summary: Roughly 40–50% of insomnia patients have comorbid anxiety or depression; treat both dimensions (AASM).
key_points: Anxiety/depression can trigger insomnia; insomnia worsens anxiety/depression
CBT-I remains effective in comorbid cases
If mood symptoms are severe, prioritize psychiatric evaluation
PHQ-9 and GAD-7 are screening references (AI does not diagnose)

guidelines.summary: Older adults' sleep architecture changes are partly physiological; treatment is calibrated (AASM).
key_points: Modest reduction in total sleep time is normal aging — doesn't always need treatment
BzRAs raise fall and cognitive-impairment risk significantly — prefer CBT-I
Short (≤30 min) afternoon naps may be allowed
Morning light exposure is especially important for circadian rhythm in older adults

guidelines.summary: Acute insomnia (<3 months) is often stress-driven and self-limiting; chronic insomnia is explained by the 3P model (Predisposing + Precipitating + Perpetuating) and needs active intervention.
key_points: Acute insomnia: address the precipitant (stress, jet lag); CBT-I not necessarily required immediately
Chronic insomnia's perpetuating factors are CBT-I's main target: prolonged bedtime, daytime naps, sleep over-vigilance, sleep-specific dysfunctional beliefs (see DBAS)
About 30% of acute insomnia becomes chronic; early CBT intervention reduces that risk
